# Storage growth — arm 4 results

*Generated by `bench/report/build-report.mjs` from the run records in
[`bench/runs/`](../runs). Do not edit by hand: re-run the script.*

**Deterministic arm.** No model, no agent, no LLM call. A seeded generator produces a
coding-agent-shaped trajectory — tool calls, model calls, messages, test results, commits — and
the arm appends it through the real server, checkpoints it, verifies it, and lands changes, on a
Postgres database created for the run and dropped after it. What it reports is what that
database then holds. `PLAN.md` 3-6's retention and tiering policy is meant to be written
against these numbers rather than against the 2026-08-22 model.

**Two content profiles, because a synthetic payload's compressibility is a choice.** `text` is
drawn from a Zipf-weighted vocabulary of code and prose and compresses the way source does;
`random` is random six-bit characters and barely compresses at all. Real content lies between
them, and every compression and dedup figure is given for both.

Environment: Postgres 16.14 (`default_toast_compression = pglz`), node v24.18.0, linux/x64, 16× 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900H @ 2.50GHz, 15 GiB. Server commit `21a45a04dd7d885d123014fb4cfa6f7bf47e8383`, run as server/dist/main.js, its own process. Seed 1; whole run 175 s.

## What this shows

- **Under the default `structure` mode an event costs 798 B, and the payload is 13.7% of it.** The rest is the row — hashes, ids, typed columns — and 291 B of index per event. Retention that ages out payloads (3-6's "verified, payload not retained") can reclaim at most that 13.7% on a default repository; the bulk of what an event costs is what keeps it verifiable and queryable.
- **At ingest scale the per-event cost holds**: 869 B/event over 200,000 events, against 798 B at 20,000. A million default events is 0.81 GiB of `session_events`.
- **`full` costs 1.63× the default on text-shaped payloads** (1,303 B/event), and TOAST stores its payloads at 576 B/event. Compressed a thousand at a time instead, the same payloads take 196 B/event — 34.0% of what is stored today. TOAST compresses one value at a time and only once a row passes ~2 KB, so 90.7% of these rows are stored uncompressed.
- **#194 alone makes no stored SBOM byte a copy.** Take out the UUID and the timestamp and every land's SBOM is still distinct, because it names the commit it describes (`metadata.component.version`). What an unchanged lockfile does repeat is the component list: 99.5% of those bytes are copies. Reclaiming them needs the component list stored once and referenced by digest, which is 3-6's shape rather than 3-3's.
- **A landed change costs 8,561 B of Postgres** and 17,121 B of git objects; its SBOM is 3,631 B of the Postgres figure (42.4%) — a 7,146 B statement, base64-encoded into a DSSE envelope and then compressed by TOAST.
- **The storage meter reads 1.72× low on `session_events`**, and 1.72× across every table here. It sums row datums by design (core/storage-usage.ts) — no index, no page overhead — so an org quota of N bytes admits roughly that multiple of N on disk.
- **Verifying the whole run — 200,000 events in 4 sessions — grew the server's resident set by 0.0 MiB** over the 454.2 MiB it already held, in 2,428 ms; anchored at checkpoints, 194 ms. #152's batched read holds one batch per session at a time, and on a warm heap that fits inside what the process already has. This shows it stayed there; it does not show what a freshly started process verifying the same run would need.
- **Ingest ran at a median 3,021 events/s** across 4 writers in batches of 200, with `session_events` growing to 280,000 rows, and its last two deciles ran at 104.4% of that median. No cliff inside that range — which bounds where one could be, and says nothing past it.

## Bytes per unit

What Postgres allocated per unit — heap, out-of-line TOAST, and indexes, as relation-size
deltas on a database only this arm wrote to — beside the row-datum sum the storage meter
counts. Free-space and visibility maps are in the total and not broken out.

| Unit | Count | Heap B | TOAST B | Index B | **Total B** | Meter B |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trajectory event — `structure`, text | 20,000 | 505 | 0 | 291 | **798** | 481 |
| Trajectory event — `structure`, random | 20,000 | 508 | 0 | 308 | **817** | 487 |
| Trajectory event — `full`, text | 20,000 | 845 | 66 | 391 | **1,303** | 876 |
| Trajectory event — `full`, random | 20,000 | 757 | 387 | 389 | **1,533** | 1,082 |
| Trajectory event — `structure`, text, 4 writers | 200,000 | 488 | 0 | 381 | **869** | 472 |
| Checkpoint | 100 | 1,311 | 1,802 | 164 | **3,523** | 2,204 |
| Operation-log row | 915 | 358 | 0 | 269 | **654** | 293 |
| Landed change (Postgres) | 200 | 2,171 | 4,301 | 1,720 | **8,561** | 5,409 |

A landed change also adds 17,121 B of git objects (`git count-objects -v`, the meter's own measure).

**The synthetic corpus beside the real one.** The `text` profile supplied a mean of 793 B per
payload; the 2026-08-22 storage analysis measured 833 B across 1,930 real events.

## Compression: realised against batched

"Uncompressed" is the payload as jsonb before TOAST; "stored" is the datum as it sits
(`pg_column_size`). The deflate columns compress the *stored* payloads with one algorithm
at every grain, so the difference between them is the batching and not the codec.

| Configuration | Uncompressed B/event | Stored B/event | Rows TOAST-compressed | Deflate, per event | Deflate, batch of 200 | Deflate, batch of 1000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `structure`, text | 111 | 109 | 0.0% | 67 | 6 | 5 |
| `structure`, random | 111 | 109 | 0.0% | 67 | 6 | 5 |
| `full`, text | 794 | 576 | 9.3% | 327 | 199 | 196 |
| `full`, random | 779 | 778 | 0.0% | 599 | 533 | 532 |

The server verifies straight after ingesting every event above, so it does so on a warm heap.
Growth is what the verify added to that.

## What this does not show

**The corpus is synthetic.** Its sizes are calibrated to the one real measurement there is, and
its content is bracketed rather than chosen, but no real trajectory went through this. Real
payloads repeat themselves across events — the same file read twice, the same tool output —
in ways a PRNG does not, so the payload dedup yields here are a floor under `full`, not an
estimate.

**One machine, one Postgres, freshly written.** Every relation was built by inserts into an empty
database and measured straight away: no updates, no deletes, no vacuum, no bloat, and indexes as
compact as they will ever be. A database that has run for a year holds the same rows in more
pages. The multiples against the meter are a lower bound for the same reason.

**Retention is not exercised.** Nothing here ages out, so "verified, payload not retained" is
priced by subtraction — the payload column's share of an event — and not by running it.

**The ingest curve stops where the run stops.** Its range is the table in the Ingest section. A
cliff past it is neither shown nor ruled out, and the rates include this box's HTTP stack and
request logging, which a production deployment shares and a differently-sized one would not.

**Peak RSS is the server process's, sampled.** It is the larger of the kernel's high-water mark
(reset before each request) and `VmRSS` polled every 5 ms, and both are approximate by a few
hundred KiB on per-CPU counters. And the server verifies straight after ingesting, with a warm
heap: growth near zero says the read stayed inside what the process already held, not what a
freshly started process verifying a large run cold would need.
